author.headline: Expert in applying AI in verification

text:
How can you convince the AI that the web page it builds is not exactly the same as the reference web page, while it insists that they look the same?

Suddenly, I understand the frustration of my wife when she tries to tell me the paint colors do not match in our renovation project where I genuinely can't notice the difference.

author.name: Monir Abdalhk
author.headline: Senior CAD DV Methodology Engineer at AMD

comments.text: What worked for me was splitting the job between different models based on what they’re actually good at. Gemini is better at interpreting screenshots and picking up visual details, so I use it to turn the reference page into a structured JSON template. Then I pass that JSON to Opus, which is much stronger at clean, accurate implementation. Once the design is written down in measurable terms, there’s no more arguing about whether things look the same.

author.name: Ganesh Krishna Garga
author.headline: SoC Design Verification Engineer at Intel Corporation

comments.text: Interesting problem. Maybe could you get the LLM to put out the criteria it used to decide that the pages are the same?

author.name: Horace Chan
author.headline: Expert in applying AI in verification

replies.text: Ganesh Krishna Garga I think I hit a fundamental limit of LLM.  LLM thinks in words.  If you turn my fake bloomberg and the real bloomberg into words only description, the words are very similar.  But subtle details are lost in the image to words translation that is very obvious to human eyes
